appraisal_events.evidence: « je vois bien que vous devez avoir les plaisirs de l'intelligence et c'est probablement ce qui compte surtout pour vous » ; puis, malgré le démenti du narrateur, « cela doit être cela que vous aimez le mieux, moi, je me le figure » ; « Il ne me persuadait certes pas ; et pourtant je me sentais plus heureux, moins à l'étroit. »
appraisal_events.explanation: Bergotte credits the narrator with a superior inner life and holds to that estimate even after the narrator denies it, and the narrating voice records the result as a real lifting of his spirits. The narrator's protest qualifies the truth of the compliment but not the local benefit he draws from it.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Surtout ce qu'il avait dit de M. de Norpois ôtait beaucoup de sa force à une condamnation que j'avais crue sans appel. » ; « selon Bergotte qui avait l'air de connaître mon cas, il semblait que le symptôme à négliger c'était au contraire mes doutes »
appraisal_events.explanation: Bergotte's remarks strip the authority from Norpois's verdict, which the narrator had taken as final; Bergotte replaces Norpois as the credible judge of the narrator's case.

status_effects.explanation: He ends the passage « plus heureux, moins à l'étroit », released from a condemnation he had believed beyond appeal — a real but qualified gain, since he explicitly remains unpersuaded.

Answering the compliment, he confesses inwardly that all lofty reasoning leaves him cold, that his desires are « purement matériel », that he would easily do without intelligence, and that his ideal life — being linked with the duchesse de Guermantes — has no room for intellectual pleasures, an avowal he dares not make aloud.
His verdict on the narrator, previously treated as « sans appel », loses much of its force once Bergotte has spoken of him.
He is granted the standing of one « qui avait l'air de connaître mon cas », and his judgment locally overrides Norpois's as the authority the narrator lives by.

ambiguities: The passage stages a contradiction it does not resolve: the narrator flatly declares Bergotte's flattering diagnosis « peu vrai pour moi », yet the closing paragraph credits Bergotte with seeming to know his case, so it is uncertain whether the compliment is endorsed as accurate or only as therapeutically effective.

Norpois's diminishment rests on remarks about him reported only at second hand (« ce qu'il avait dit de M. de Norpois »); the passage does not supply their content, so their evaluative direction is inferred from their effect.
